text: Welcome to This is My Architecture.
Today we're talking automated compliance with Alex from Dome9.
What does Dome9 do?
Dome9 is a company that's completely focused on giving you better visibility,
security, and compliance into what's going on within your public cloud infrastructure.
Very cool.
Now, what is your architecture solving from a business standpoint?
Yeah, so with the core of Dome9 today, really what we do is around giving you better visibility
into how things are going.
And so it's a lot of reporting, but what we saw from our customers is that they wanted
to take this further.
They didn't want to just be informed that something was wrong or maybe misconfigured, but they wanted
to fix it as well.
And so that's really what CloudBots is doing.
So you created this thing called CloudBots.
Talk us through the workflow here.
Yeah, absolutely.
So, the way it works is up top here, Dome9 is doing what Dome9 does.
It's bringing in information across different cloud accounts and asserting on configurations.
And what happens is then once it asserts on that configuration, if it finds something
that is out of compliance, we can notify you.
And so in this case, the way we do it is we set up Dome9 to send this information over
to SNS.
Now from here, the nice thing about SNS is that it's so flexible.
And so in this case, going from here over to Lambda is a pretty easy thing to do.
And so we set up SNS to trigger this function.
And this function is really where all of the work is actually done.
So that's the CloudBot in the function.
That is the CloudBot, yeah.
And that's the nice thing is that it's one function that has all of the CloudBots within
it.
It's just one function overall.
And so this function, again, that's where the work is done.
And so what it does is it takes the message from SNS and first thing it does is just has
to parse it.
It says, okay, well, what happened?
Where did this thing break?
How did it break?
What's the supporting information about this particular service or object?
And then what do I want to do with it?
And once it does all of those kind of parsing and looking through that information, assuming
it knows what to do and where to do it, it goes and runs that remediation action.
And it can either go and run the remediation locally within the account that it's running,
or what we're seeing a lot of our customers do is having this Lambda assume a role over
to their other accounts.
Because at the end of the day, the environments that we're looking at are significant.
And if you have hundreds or thousands of accounts, you don't want to maintain even this small
stack across that whole environment.
Yeah.
Instead, we have one function that takes care of that across the whole entire environment.
And so once any action or remediation happens, what's happening down here?
Yeah.
The rest of it is really logging.
You know, Dome9, again, it's already generating reports.
So you'll get information from them saying, hey, here's something that we found.
But at the same time, we also want to know how this went and make sure it worked and that
there wasn't anything odd happening.
And so once Lambda goes and finishes up running that remediation wherever it is, it then goes
and outputs over to SNS.
Again, SNS is so flexible.
And so from here, we can really send this wherever we want to go.
Especially just setting up.
Email is an easy thing.
Yeah.
But on an ongoing basis, we probably also want to send this over to Slack.
Probably want to log it in our Sumos and Splunks of the world.
Wherever it is that you send this information, we can get there with SNS.
And if you use Lambda here, what language did you use to implement the CloudBot?
Yeah.
It's written in Python.
The nice thing about Boto3 is that there's examples everywhere.
It's beautifully documented.
And it really allows us to build out these bots but without having a ton of support in
code.
Everything is really nice and concise.
And I noticed you've got GuardDuty here.
How have you worked that into what Dome9 is doing?
Yeah.
Yeah.
So what we saw is that, again, the real challenge in this is having Dome9 assert on these configurations
and tell us what's good and bad.
And the actual remediation, although it's very impactful, by itself, it doesn't need to be
from Dome9 that we might want to quarantine a bucket or lock down an instance or something
like that.
And so we had some customers say, well, hey, if we've already got this framework, what else
can I do with this?
And GuardDuty came to mind as a really good service to run the same kind of remediation
with.
So the way this works is that just like Dome9 is asserting on configurations and telling
us when something bad happens, GuardDuty does the same thing.
And it says, hey, you're mining Bitcoin in Brazil.
That's something that we probably don't want to be doing.
And then via CloudWatch events, again, we end back up over an SNS and the same workflow
completes.
So you've got reuse across multiple inputs.
Yeah.
And that's really the goal is we didn't want to black box this.
Everybody is writing some sort of remediation on their own.
And instead, we want to say, hey, here is a service that is really something that we
can build and tack onto as much as possible.
Because everyone's trying to do some sort of remediation.
And is this stack running in a Dome9 account or the customer's account?
How does that work?
Yeah.
It's running in the customer account, which is really important because with Dome9 and
the size and type of customers that we're really working with, they have very sensitive
data.
And even giving read access to anyone is a big deal.
But then when you start asking for the kind of write permissions that Lambda needs to run
these actions, they don't want to give it to any third party.
We don't want those rights anyways.
So instead, from Dome9, all it's doing, again, is asserting on those configurations and sending
it off to SNS.
But all the permissions and all of those sorts of things live on that execution role in that
function.
And because you've used Lander, it's all serverless here.
I'm assuming scale is not an issue.
Yeah.

That's a very nice thing.
Well, it sounds like a great solution for our customers.
Alex, thanks so much for joining us today.
